questions.question: In the course's terminology, which description defines a path in a network?
options: A sequence of edges from a start to an end vertex that never visits any vertex twice
A set of edges that each touch the start vertex or the end vertex of the route
A sequence of distinct edges from start to end vertex, consecutive edges sharing a vertex
A sequence of edges from a start to an end vertex, where an edge may be used repeatedly

questions.question: Under the course's definition of a path as a sequence of distinct edges, may a path visit the same vertex twice?
options: No, since every vertex may appear only once
Yes, but only the start vertex, at the very end
Yes, and then edges at that vertex may repeat too
Yes, as long as no edge is used a second time

questions.question: In a path, how must two consecutive edges in the sequence be related?
options: They must have equal lengths so the route is balanced
They must both have the start vertex of the path as an end
They share a vertex: the first ends where the next begins
They may be anywhere, as long as both belong to the network

questions.question: A network contains the edge $A\text{-}B$. Under the course's definition of a path as a sequence of distinct edges connecting a starting vertex to an ending vertex, with consecutive edges sharing a vertex, is the single edge $A\text{-}B$ on its own a path from $A$ to $B$?
options: No; a path needs two or more edges, so that consecutive edges share a vertex
No; a path has to pass through some vertex other than its two end vertices
Yes; the one-edge sequence $A\text{-}B$ joins the start $A$ to the end $B$
Yes, but only when the edge $A\text{-}B$ carries a numerical length value

questions.question: A network has edges $A\text{-}B=4$, $A\text{-}C=2$, $B\text{-}C=1$, $B\text{-}D=5$, $C\text{-}D=8$, $C\text{-}E=10$, $D\text{-}E=2$, $D\text{-}F=6$, $E\text{-}F=3$ (lengths), usable both ways. What is the length of the path $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}E\text{-}D\text{-}F$?

A network has the two-way edges $A\text{-}B$, $A\text{-}C$, $B\text{-}C$, $B\text{-}D$, $C\text{-}D$, $C\text{-}E$, $D\text{-}E$, $D\text{-}F$ and $E\text{-}F$. Which vertex sequence is a path from $A$ to $F$?
options: $A\text{-}D\text{-}F$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}B\text{-}D\text{-}F$
$A\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}F$
$C\text{-}D\text{-}F$

questions.question: A directed network has the edges $A\to B$, $B\to C$, $C\to D$ and $D\to B$, each usable only in its direction. Which vertex sequence is a path?
options: $A\to B\to D\to C$
$A\to B\to C\to B$
$B\to C\to D\to B\to C$
$A\to B\to C\to D\to B$

questions.question: A path is written as the vertex sequence $A\text{-}C\text{-}B\text{-}D$. Which edges does it use, in order?
options: $A\text{-}C$ and $B\text{-}D$
$A\text{-}C$, $A\text{-}B$, $A\text{-}D$
$A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$
$A\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}D$

questions.question: In a network whose edges are usable both ways and carry lengths, a path from $u$ to $v$ has length $\ell$. What is the length of the reversed vertex sequence from $v$ to $u$?
options: $\ell$, because the same edges and lengths are used
Not defined, since a path has a fixed start vertex
$-\ell$, since every edge is traversed the other way
$\ell$ only if the path visits no vertex twice

questions.question: In a directed network, $u=v_0\to v_1\to\dots\to v_k=v$ is a path. When is the reversed sequence $v_k,v_{k-1},\dots,v_0$ a path from $v$ to $u$?
options: Always, since its edges are the same distinct edges as in the original path
Never, since a path in a directed network cannot be reversed
When the path visits each of its vertices $v_0,\dots,v_k$ at most once
When for each edge $v_{i-1}\to v_i$ the edge $v_i\to v_{i-1}$ also exists

questions.question: In a network with edge lengths, a route from $u$ to $v$ uses distinct edges, consecutive ones sharing a vertex, but other such routes from $u$ to $v$ are shorter. Is the route a path?
options: Yes; whether a route is a path does not depend on its length
No; a path is a route of the smallest possible length
Only if it uses fewer edges than any other route from $u$ to $v$
Only if no vertex is visited twice along the route

questions.question: A network has the two-way edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}A$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}E$ and $E\text{-}C$. Which route is a path in the course's sense but not in the graph-theory sense with distinct vertices?
options: $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}E\text{-}C$
$A\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}E\text{-}C\text{-}A$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}B$

questions.question: A directed network has the edges $S\to A=2$, $A\to B=3$, $B\to S=1$, $S\to B=7$ and $B\to T=4$ (lengths). What is the length of the path $S\to A\to B\to S\to B\to T$?

Using a network's two-way edges $P\text{-}Q$, $Q\text{-}R$, $Q\text{-}S$ and $R\text{-}S$, a student writes the route $P\text{-}Q\text{-}R\text{-}Q\text{-}S$ and calls it a path from $P$ to $S$. Is the student right?
options: Yes; $Q\text{-}R$ and $R\text{-}Q$ are two different edges
No; it is not, because vertex $Q$ appears twice
No; it uses the edge $Q\text{-}R$ twice, once each way
Yes; every vertex in the sequence is in the network

questions.question: A network has $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. Under the course definition of a path, which bound on the number of edges of a path is correct?
options: At most $n-1$, since a path visits each vertex once
At most $m$, and it can exceed $n-1$ when vertices repeat
No bound, since vertices may be visited repeatedly
Exactly $m$, since a path must use every edge of the network

questions.question: Path $P_1$ runs from $u$ to $v$ and path $P_2$ from $v$ to $w$, with lengths $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$. Exactly when is $P_1$ followed by $P_2$ a path from $u$ to $w$, of length $\ell_1+\ell_2$?
options: When $P_1$ and $P_2$ share no vertex except $v$
Always, since $P_1$ and $P_2$ are paths already
When $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ are both positive
When no edge of $P_1$ is also an edge of $P_2$

questions.question: A network has the two-way edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}B$ and $B\text{-}E$, and $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}B\text{-}E$ is a path from $A$ to $E$. Which route from $A$ to $E$ uses only edges of this path and visits no vertex twice?
options: $A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}B\text{-}E$, the given path itself
$A\text{-}B\text{-}E$, cutting out the loop $B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}B$
$A\text{-}B\text{-}D\text{-}C\text{-}B\text{-}E$, taking the loop the other way
$A\text{-}B\text{-}C\text{-}D\text{-}E$, dropping the return to $B$
